edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page instead of a bare right-aligned page number.

edits.quote: Blocks must fit inside the thick line and sit on the thin lines.
edits.fix: 'Sit on the thin lines' can be heard as straddling the lines. Say 'Each block covers whole small triangles. Blocks stay inside the thick line and may not overlap.'

edits.quote: Find all the ways to cover each shape with blue blocks. Make every shape a different way.
edits.fix: Say what counts as different and how to record it, e.g. 'Cover the small hexagon in a different way on each copy, and the long hexagon in a different way on each copy. Draw the blocks.' (The numbers of copies, 2 and 3, already match the numbers of coverings.)

edits.quote: Find all the ways to cover each shape on this page and the next with blue blocks. Make every shape a different way.
edits.fix: Make the same rewrite as in P3 and tell children to draw each covering. They cannot leave 8 blocks on each of six boards, so without drawing there is no record of which coverings they have found.

k-1.summary: Six concrete problems on actual-size boards, all correct: possible and impossible shapes (including an 8-triangle trapezoid that cannot be covered), fewest greens in triangles of side 2-4 (answers 2, 3, 4), all coverings of small hexagons (2, 3 and 6 coverings with exactly that many copies), fewest blocks (3, 3, 4), and a block-placing game whose winners are 1, 2, 1, 1, 2. It gives a quick child about forty minutes. The only edits needed are saying how to record the 'find all the ways' coverings, a clearer placement rule, and the footer.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.

edits.quote: Cover each board with blue rhombuses, or decide that it cannot be done. For each board that cannot be covered, explain why.
edits.fix: This repeats Problem 1 word for word, and the board letters already continue from A-D to E-G. Fold boards E-G into Problem 1 ('on this page and the next') and keep only 'The gray triangles are holes and are not part of the board.'

edits.quote: Find a rule that tells which places for the two green triangles work, and explain why your rule is right.
edits.fix: The rule is correct: all 144 one-up/one-down placements can be completed. But proving that every such placement works is beyond grades 2-3. Ask them to explain why the placements that fail cannot work, and leave the sufficiency argument (for example, a closed path through all 24 triangles) to the adult.

grades-2-3.summary: This band develops kernel 1 well, and every board checks out: A and D can be covered, B (odd area) and C (7 up, 5 down) cannot; E (two up-holes) and F (bowtie) cannot, G can. The fewest greens are 2, 3, 4, 5, versus 4, 5, 4, 5 with chevrons, and a 19-triangle board with 12 up and 7 down exists. The packet then ends with a design problem and a rule-finding problem. Edits are light: one repeated instruction, an over-reaching 'explain why your rule is right', and the footer.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.

edits.quote: Give each of your coverings in Problem 1 a letter.
edits.fix: Use numbers 1-6 instead. Problem 3 uses A-F for coverings of a different board, and Problems 4 and 6 refer back to those letters.

edits.quote: Find a way to do this with 4 flips that never flips the same hexagon twice in a row. (followed by two writing lines)
edits.fix: Replace the two lines with a small copy of covering A (or a strip of small hexagons) where children mark or number the hexagons they flip, so the 4-flip loop can be recorded and checked.

edits.quote: On the hexagon board each covering has two ribbons, because its top side has two short edges.
edits.fix: Write 'On the hexagon board from Problem 3'. The Problem 1 board is also a hexagon, and it has only one ribbon.

edits.quote: Problem 7: How many different coverings does the hexagon board from Problem 3 have?
edits.fix: Swap P7 and P8. The 1-3-3 board in P8 has a single ribbon, so its 20 coverings follow directly from P5 (arrangements of LLLRRR). The side-2 hexagon (also 20) needs two ribbons that interact, so it makes the harder last problem.

grades-4-5.summary: This band develops kernel 2 well and every claim checks out. P1's board has 6 coverings, and P2's flip graph has diameter 4. The flip distances in P3 are 3, 4 and 8, verified by search, with E and F the two extreme coverings. In P4 a 4-flip loop exists and 5 or 7 flips is impossible. The ribbon diagram LRRLR is drawn correctly, and P7 and P8 both have 20 coverings. Edits are light: a letter clash, naming the board in P5, recording space for P4, and the order of P7 and P8.

overall.strongest: Grades 2-3 builds the up/down counting argument through a well-chosen and fully correct run of boards, from possible and impossible boards to fewest greens with a proof, chevrons, inventing a board, and finding a rule.
overall.weakest: K-1 is the thinnest mathematically, and its two 'find all the ways' problems never say how to record coverings, though it is concrete, correct, and long enough for the hour.
